summary: Explains how IGMPv3 and MLDv2 let hosts tell neighboring routers they want to receive multicast traffic, and how they support source-specific multicast, where a host asks for traffic from a particular sender. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: You can ask to hear only from one speaker. This explains how a device tells the nearby router which sender it wants.

questions: what is the ssm address range
subtitle: How IGMPv3 and MLDv2 hosts and routers should behave when a receiver asks for traffic from one specific sender.

tldr.problem: Source-specific multicast needs receivers to name both a sender and a group, but IGMPv3 and MLDv2 were written to also allow older, any-source behavior, which can undermine SSM.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines SSM-aware hosts and routers that know the SSM address range, and tightens the rules: hosts avoid EXCLUDE-mode records for SSM addresses, and routers ignore EXCLUDE-mode and older-version reports for them.
tldr.outcome: SSM destination addresses are handled only with source-specific semantics, and an attacker cannot push a link into older-version compatibility mode to deny SSM service. The RFC updates RFC 3376 and RFC 3810.

today: RFC 4604 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 3376 and RFC 3810.

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) lets an IPv4 host tell its neighboring routers which multicast groups it wants. IGMP version 3 adds the ability to request or filter traffic from individual sources within a group. The Multicast Listener Discovery Protocol (MLD) does the same job for IPv6, and MLD version 2 adds the analogous source filtering.

The RFC uses GMP for IGMP and MLD together, and SFGMP (Source Filtering GMP) for IGMPv3 and MLDv2 together. The general requirements for the SSM service model live in RFC 4607. This document applies them concretely to IGMPv3 and MLDv2, and it updates both specifications.

Changes to the base protocols are tagged MODIFICATION. Everything else is a clarification of existing behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts and routers already have a way to talk about who wants which broadcast. This paper adds extra rules for the case where you ask for one particular sender only.

sections.title: SSM-Aware Hosts and the Address Range
sections.content:
A host that knows the SSM address range and can apply SSM semantics to it is called SSM-aware. IANA allocates 232/8 for SSM in IPv4. In IPv6 the FF3x::/32 range is reserved for SSM semantics, where x is a valid multicast scope value, although current allocations are restricted to FF3x::/96.

A host or router may be configured to apply SSM semantics to other ranges. The GMP module SHOULD offer a configuration option for the SSM range, and if it does, the option MUST default to the IANA-allocated range. The mechanism MUST at least allow manual configuration.

If an SSM-aware host receives a request from an application that is not source-specific for an SSM destination address, the host IP module SHOULD return an error, as specified in RFC 3678. On a host that is not SSM-aware, an application using the wrong API gets no useful signal: an SSM-aware router will refuse the request and the traffic simply never arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a special set of channel numbers reserved for "pick your sender" shows. If you ask for one of those without naming a sender, the computer should tell you that was a mistake.

sections.title: Host Behavior for Reports and Queries
sections.content:
An SSM-aware host may report several SSM channels (a source and group pair) in one report. For an SSM address, the normal record types are MODE_IS_INCLUDE in a Current-State Record, and ALLOW_NEW_SOURCES or BLOCK_OLD_SOURCES in a State-Change Record. A single report may also mix SSM and non-source-specific (ASM) addresses. A host may send CHANGE_TO_INCLUDE_MODE in some cases, for example when the SSM range is changed by configuration.

A host SHOULD NOT send MODE_IS_EXCLUDE or CHANGE_TO_EXCLUDE_MODE for an SSM address, because EXCLUDE mode does not apply there. This is a modification.

If an IGMPv1 Query, or an IGMPv2 or MLDv1 General Query, arrives, the base specifications make the host fall back to the older version on that interface. The host then reports interest in the whole group without a source, and the router stops applying SSM semantics. A compliant router never sends such a query for an SSM address, so this only happens if the router is not SSM-aware or the two disagree about the SSM range. The host SHOULD log an error, and it SHOULD also log one for an IGMPv2 or MLDv1 Group Specific Query in an SSM range.

Queries that are source-specific work as before. A host must answer a Group-Specific Query if the group matches any subscribed channel, and must answer a Group-and-Source-Specific Query when both group and source match a subscription, including queries listing multiple sources.

Hosts in older-version compatibility mode MUST NOT let another host's older-version report suppress their own report. Suppression would let an attacker deny SSM service to other hosts on the link.
sections.plainLanguage: If the router starts talking in an old, simpler language, the host should write down that something is wrong. It should also keep speaking up for itself instead of staying quiet because someone else spoke.

sections.title: Router Behavior
sections.content:
An SSM-aware router knows the SSM range and applies SSM semantics to it. If it can be configured with other ranges, the default MUST be the IANA-allocated range.

For reports, a router SHOULD ignore any MODE_IS_EXCLUDE or CHANGE_TO_EXCLUDE_MODE record that refers to an SSM address, MAY log an error, and MUST still process the other records in the same report. This keeps non-source-specific semantics out of SSM addresses and avoids reverting to older-version compatibility mode. A CHANGE_TO_INCLUDE_MODE record is processed by the normal rules.

Likewise, a router SHOULD ignore IGMPv1/v2 and MLDv1 reports for an SSM address and SHOULD NOT use them to create forwarding state. It SHOULD ignore IGMPv2 Leave and MLDv1 Done messages in the SSM range too. It MAY log an error in both cases.

General Queries are sent as usual. Group-Specific Queries for SSM addresses are not prohibited, although a router following RFC 3376 and RFC 3810 would not send one when this was written. Group-and-Source-Specific Queries are sent normally, typically after a BLOCK_OLD_SOURCES record, to check whether any host on the link still wants that channel. A router that loses querier election to a lower-version router must log an error, as the base specifications already require.
sections.plainLanguage: The router should only accept requests that name a sender. If someone asks the old way, the router ignores it rather than guessing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says its modifications are not known to create security concerns beyond those already present when IGMPv3 or MLDv2 are used for ASM-style multicast. SSM-specific security issues are analyzed in RFC 4607.

The key point is that a router must not accept non-source-specific reception requests for an SSM address. The base rules would make the router revert to older-version compatibility mode for that group, which would stop IGMPv3-capable hosts from getting SSM service for it. An attacker on the same link could use that to deny service to other hosts. Ignoring those requests closes that door.
sections.plainLanguage: If a router could be tricked into using the old, simple rules, a troublemaker could spoil things for everyone nearby. Ignoring the trick stops that.

sections.title: What This Updates
sections.content:
The RFC is a Standards Track document that updates RFC 3376 (IGMPv3) and RFC 3810 (MLDv2). It builds on RFC 4607, the general SSM specification, and refers to RFC 3678 for socket interface behavior and RFC 3306 for the IPv6 address range.

Implementers mainly need to know three things: how to recognize SSM addresses, which record types to avoid or ignore there, and which conditions to log as errors.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper is an add-on to two older rulebooks. It adds a few new rules without replacing them.
